\section[condemnō, condemnāre]{condemnō, condemnāre — to condemn, to find guilty}

\label{lesson:LA-C413-condemno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an informer, then the Latin for a defence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: condemnō, condemnāre}
\textbf{condemnō, condemnāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to condemn, to find guilty\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Iūdicēs eum furtī condemnāvērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The judges found him guilty of theft.}
\end{quote}

\emph{condemnō, condemnāre, condemnāvī, condemnātum}, with the charge in the genitive. English \emph{condemn}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{condemnō} is built from \emph{con-} and \emph{damnō} \textquotedblleft{}to condemn\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), which comes from \emph{damnum} \textquotedblleft{}a loss, a fine\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{condemn} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{condemnō, condemnāre}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{condemnō, condemnāre}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{condemnō, condemnāre}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for an informer, then the Latin for a defence, then say \emph{condemnō, condemnāre} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[damnātiō, damnātiōnis]{damnātiō, damnātiōnis — a conviction, a condemnation}

\label{lesson:LA-C413-damnatio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a defence, then the Latin for to condemn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: damnātiō, damnātiōnis}
\textbf{damnātiō, damnātiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}a conviction, a condemnation\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Post damnātiōnem in exsilium iit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After his conviction he went into exile.}
\end{quote}

\emph{damnātiō, damnātiōnis} f., the noun of \emph{damnō}. English \emph{damnation}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{damnātiō} is the noun built on \emph{damnō} \textquotedblleft{}to condemn\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), from \emph{damnum} \textquotedblleft{}a loss\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{damnation} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[absolūtiō, absolūtiōnis]{absolūtiō, absolūtiōnis — an acquittal}

\label{lesson:LA-C413-absolutio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to condemn, then the Latin for a conviction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: absolūtiō, absolūtiōnis}
\textbf{absolūtiō, absolūtiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}an acquittal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Post absolūtiōnem domum rediit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After his acquittal he went home.}
\end{quote}

\emph{absolūtiō, absolūtiōnis} f., the noun of \emph{absolvō}, to set loose. English \emph{absolution}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{absolūtiō} is the noun built on \emph{absolvō} \textquotedblleft{}to set loose, to acquit\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), from \emph{ab} and \emph{solvō} \textquotedblleft{}to loosen\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{absolution} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[dēprecor, dēprecārī]{dēprecor, dēprecārī — to beg to be spared, to plead against}

\label{lesson:LA-C413-deprecor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a conviction, then the Latin for an acquittal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēprecor, dēprecārī}
\textbf{dēprecor, dēprecārī} — \textquotedblleft{}to beg to be spared, to plead against\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Reus poenam dēprecātus est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The accused begged to be spared the punishment.}
\end{quote}

Deponent: \emph{dēprecor, dēprecārī, dēprecātus sum}, \emph{dē} + \emph{precor}, to pray: to pray a thing away. English \emph{deprecate}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dēprecor} is built from \emph{dē} \textquotedblleft{}away\textquotedblright{} and \emph{precor} \textquotedblleft{}to pray\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): to pray a thing away. English \emph{deprecate} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[patrōcinium, patrōciniī]{patrōcinium, patrōciniī — defence in court, advocacy; protection}

\label{lesson:LA-C413-patrocinium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an acquittal, then the Latin for to beg to be spared.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: patrōcinium, patrōciniī}
\textbf{patrōcinium, patrōciniī} — \textquotedblleft{}defence in court, advocacy; protection\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Patrōcinium causidicī reum nōn adiūvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The advocate's defence did not help the accused.}
\end{quote}

\emph{patrōcinium, patrōciniī} n., built on \emph{patrōnus}: the patron's protection, and his pleading in court.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{patrōcinium} is built on \emph{patrōnus} \textquotedblleft{}a patron, a defender\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), which comes from \emph{pater} \textquotedblleft{}a father\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
